newsitem.title: FRANCE: French assembly approves tighter immigration law.
newsitem.headline: French assembly approves tighter immigration law.

text.p: France's National Assembly passed a bill on Thursday to tighten already tough laws against illegal immigration, despite opposition complaints that it violated civil liberties.

With unemployment at a record high and the far-right National Front gaining strength on complaints that immigrants are taking jobs from "native-born" French people, it approved even stricter reforms than the centre-right government had proposed.

Opposition socialist and communist members voted against the measure, which now goes to the Senate. "We are vigorously, totally opposed to this bill, which is contrary to fundamental liberties," said socialist deputy Jacques Guyard.
The bill is part of efforts by Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre to crack down on the estimated one million illegal immigrants among France's five million foreigners.

The government triggered a national controversy earlier this year when it ordered police to forcibly evict more than 200 Africans, mostly without residence papers, from their refuge in a Paris church.
The new law sought by Debre would prevent a repeat of the situation when magistrates later thwarted orders expelling most of them.
Human rights activists accuse Debre of lacking sensitivity while ultra-leftists want Paris to offer blanket asylum to all foreigners now in France.
The National Front led by Jean-Marie Le Pen, backed by about 15 percent of the electorate, wants to expel millions of foreigners, including even those legally residing in France.
One controversial provision of the bill passed by the assembly would limit an individual's freedom to put up a foreigner temporarily in a private residence.
Another would bar an illegal immigrant unconditionally from obtaining a residence permit, no matter how long the immigrant had lived in France.

The bill would also allow police to fingerprint foreigners from outside the European Union asking to visit France, so that police could better track down visitors who decided to remain in France without the necessary papers.
It would double to two years the time required for the foreign spouse of a French national to obtain permanent residence rights.

Police say this would stop fake weddings in which foreigners offer money to poor French people to marry them, allowing them to enter the country legally, then divorce and bring their own families to France.
